title: IYT Flotilla Skipper
note: Scenario questions written for study, close to the IYT Flotilla Skipper syllabus. Not official IYT exam content. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults to verify.

questions.q: You engage astern from rest. Which way does the stern kick?
options: To port
Towards the nearer pontoon
Neither — she backs straight
To starboard
questions.why: A right-handed propeller walks the stern to port when going astern.

questions.q: You must turn the boat round in this fairway. Which way do you turn?
options: Either way — prop walk has no effect
To starboard — prop walk astern helps
To port — prop walk astern helps
To port — the rudder works best that way
questions.why: Astern, a right-handed prop kicks the stern to port, which swings the bow to starboard.

questions.q: Leaving the pontoon, you steer to starboard to move away. What does your stern do?

figure.title: Leaving along the pontoon
lines: Pontoon close on your port side

options: Follows the bow out to starboard
Stays put; only the bow moves
Swings to port, towards the pontoon
Swings to starboard, away from it
questions.why: Going ahead a boat pivots well forward, so the stern swings the opposite way to the bow.

questions.q: You are drifting almost stopped, engine in neutral, and turn the wheel hard over. Why does the boat not turn?
options: The rudder only works in reverse
The wheel must turn twice as far
The keel stops her turning at rest
No water is flowing past the rudder
questions.why: A rudder steers only when water flows over it — from boat speed or prop wash.

questions.q: You are stopped in a marina and want the bow to swing to starboard without gathering speed. What do you do?
options: Wheel to starboard, short burst ahead
Wheel to starboard, steady slow astern
Wheel amidships, long burst ahead
Wheel to port, short burst ahead
questions.why: Prop wash over the turned rudder swings the boat before she picks up way.

questions.q: You are reversing down the fairway when the wheel suddenly spins out of your hand and the boat swerves. What should you have done?
options: Gone astern faster to steer better
Held the wheel firmly and gone slower
Locked the wheel with the autopilot
Let the wheel centre itself
questions.why: Going astern the rudder tries to slam over; hold the wheel firmly and keep the speed low.

questions.q: You slow right down in this fairway. What does the bow do?
options: Holds straight — the keel stops it
Turns up into the wind, to starboard
Blows off downwind, to port
Stays put while the stern blows off
questions.why: At low speed the high bow catches more wind than the keel can resist, so it blows off downwind.

questions.q: You are about to come alongside the fuel berth. How fast do you approach?
options: Any speed — the fenders take the knock
At cruising speed, to keep steering
Fast, then full astern at the last moment
No faster than you'd want to hit it
questions.why: Approach at a speed you could accept hitting at — slow, with just enough way to steer.

questions.q: You use the bow thruster to push the bow off the pontoon. How do you use it?
options: In short bursts, with pauses between
Switched rapidly left and right
Only at cruising speed, to help a turn
Held on until you are well clear
questions.why: Bow thrusters overheat and cut out if run for long; use short bursts.

questions.q: You reverse out of this berth. How do you start?

figure.title: Bow-in finger berth
lines: Neighbour close on your port side

options: Ahead first, to swing the stern to port
Gently astern, letting the rudder take over
Wheel hard over first, then full astern
A hard burst astern to get out quickly
questions.why: Prop walk is strongest from rest at high revs; go gently so way builds and the rudder steers.

questions.q: You can lie either side of this pontoon and will stop with a touch of astern. Which side do you choose?
options: Starboard side to — astern pulls the stern in
Port side to — astern pushes the stern out
Port side to — astern pulls the stern in
Either — prop walk only acts from rest
questions.why: Going astern to stop, a right-handed prop walks the stern to port — onto a port-side berth.

questions.q: A boat is leaving a berth ahead and you must wait in this fairway. How do you hold position?

figure.title: Waiting to enter
lines: Wind F4 straight down the fairway

options: Circling the fairway at cruising speed
Beam-on to the wind, in neutral
In neutral, letting her drift
Head to wind, with short bursts ahead
questions.why: Head to wind the bow cannot blow off, and short bursts ahead hold you in place.

questions.q: You are coming alongside here. How do you approach?

figure.title: Coming alongside
lines: Wind F4 blowing off the pontoon

options: At a steeper angle, getting a line on fast
Parallel, stopping off to drift in
Very slowly, in neutral from far out
Stern first, with plenty of speed
questions.why: When the wind blows you off, come in at a steeper angle and get the bow line on quickly.

questions.q: You are reversing slowly down this fairway with the wind on your port beam. What do you expect?
options: The stern swings to starboard, downwind
The stern swings to port, into the wind
The bow swings to port, into the wind
She backs straight; the two cancel out
questions.why: The bow blows off downwind and prop walk kicks the stern to port: both swing the stern to port.

questions.q: You are motoring slowly ahead and need to go astern. How do you shift?
options: Stop the engine, then restart astern
Straight from ahead into astern
Pause in neutral, then engage astern
Rev up in neutral, then go astern
questions.why: A pause in neutral lets the propeller slow down and saves the gearbox.

questions.q: You are turning to starboard in your own length. After the short burst ahead, what comes next?
options: A long burst astern to build sternway
Wheel to port, then full ahead
Engine off — let the wind finish it
Neutral, short burst astern, wheel unchanged
questions.why: Short bursts ahead and astern turn her in her own length; prop walk astern adds to the turn.

questions.q: Coming into your berth, a gust pushes you off line towards a neighbour's bow. What do you do?
options: Abort, motor clear and try again
Stop there and wait for the gust to pass
Fend off with a foot between boats
Push on faster to force your way in
questions.why: If an approach goes wrong, go round again — never fend off with hands or feet.

questions.q: Going astern at 2 knots, you want the stern to move to starboard. Which way do you turn the wheel?
options: To port — the stern goes against the wheel
To starboard — the stern follows the wheel
Either way — it makes no difference astern
Amidships, and wait for prop walk
questions.why: With a wheel, going astern the stern moves the way you turn the wheel.

questions.q: Your crew want to motor in fast "so the wind can't push us about". What is your call?

figure.title: Entering the marina
lines: Narrow fairways, boats on both sides

options: Cruising speed, thruster on all the way
Dead slow in neutral, drifting through
Just enough speed to steer, no more
Fast, to be through before it acts
questions.why: Too slow and the wind takes the bow; too fast and you cannot stop — keep just steerage way.

questions.q: You reverse out of this berth and turn down the fairway. What do you watch most closely?

figure.title: Reversing out
lines: Neighbours' bows close on both sides
You steer the stern to port

options: Nothing — she backs out straight
Your bow swinging to port
Your stern swinging to starboard
Your bow swinging to starboard
questions.why: Going astern the pivot point moves aft, so the bow swings wide the opposite way to the stern.

questions.q: You are anchoring on sand in 5 m. How do you let the chain go?
options: Pay it out as the boat drifts back
Drop it all at once in a heap
Lower the anchor, keep the rest aboard
Pay it out while motoring ahead
questions.why: Laying the chain along the bottom as you move astern lets the anchor dig in.

questions.q: You look down through clear water to pick a spot. Where do you drop the anchor?

figure.note: Seen through clear water, depth 5–7 m

options: B — the weed cushions the chain
A — on the sand
B — in the thick weed
C — on the flat rock
questions.why: Sand gives good holding; anchors skate on weed and cannot dig into rock.

questions.q: Going stern-to in a marina, your crew pick up the lazy line at the stern. What do they do with it?
options: Cleat it at the stern with the stern line
Hold it by hand until you leave
Walk it forward and cleat it at the bow
Drop it once the stern lines are on
questions.why: The lazy line replaces your anchor: lead it forward and cleat it tight at the bow.

questions.q: The anchor is down and the chain laid out. How do you make sure it is holding?
options: Jerk the chain by hand at the bow
Motor ahead over it to press it in
Wait — it will dig in by itself overnight
Go astern gently, then harder, watching a transit
questions.why: Set the anchor with steady astern power; a fixed transit ashore shows if you are moving.

questions.q: You are going stern-to here. Where do you let go the anchor?
options: About 3–4 boat lengths off the quay
About one boat length off the quay
About half a length off the quay
About ten boat lengths off the quay
questions.why: Three to four lengths out leaves enough chain on the bottom to hold you off the quay.

questions.q: Reversing stern-to the quay with your anchor down, when do you take the chain up tight?
options: As soon as the anchor hits the bottom
Once the stern lines are made fast
Only if the wind gets up overnight
Before the crew throw the stern lines
questions.why: Pay out freely while reversing; with the stern lines on, tighten the chain to hold you off.

questions.q: Leaving the quay in the morning, your windlass lifts a neighbour's chain hooked over your anchor. What do you do?
options: Motor hard ahead to drag both free
Motor astern to pull yours out from under
Hold their chain on a line, lower yours clear
Keep winching until both anchors are up
questions.why: Take the other chain's weight on a slip line, drop your anchor clear, then slip the line.

questions.q: Lying alongside the town quay, the wash from passing boats makes you surge fore and aft. Which lines stop it?
options: The breast lines
The bow and stern lines
Extra fenders along the side
The springs
questions.why: Springs run fore and aft along the quay and stop the boat surging forward and back.

questions.q: You need to get the stern out first. How do you leave?

figure.title: Alongside the quay
lines: Wind F4 pinning you onto the quay

options: Ahead against a bow spring, bow fendered
Ahead against a stern spring, stern fendered
Astern against a bow spring, bow fendered
Push the stern off by hand, then go ahead
questions.why: Motoring ahead against a spring from the bow pivots the bow in and swings the stern out.

questions.q: You choose a spot for the night. Where do you anchor?
options: C — off the west end, in open water
B — in the lee, south of the island
A — the wind will hold you off the shore
A — close under the north shore
questions.why: Anchor in the lee of the land; a north wind blows onto the north shore and across open water.

questions.q: Is this a good place to drop your anchor?

figure.title: Crowded bay, Sivota
lines: Depth 5 m, you plan 25 m of chain

options: Yes — 30 m is more than your length
Yes — boats on chain swing together
No — your swinging circles overlap
Yes, if you lay less chain to fit
questions.why: In shifting wind boats swing differently; leave room for both swinging circles.

questions.q: What is happening, and what do you do?

figure.title: 02:30 at anchor
lines: Track: arcs, then a line downwind

options: You are swinging — go back to bed
The GPS lost its fix — reset it
The alarm radius is small — enlarge it
You are dragging — start the engine
questions.why: A straight track downwind away from the swinging arcs means the anchor is dragging.

questions.q: How do you lie here for the night?

figure.title: Narrow cove, Turkey
lines: Too narrow to swing at anchor

options: Anchor out, stern line to a rock or tree
Two anchors off the bow, no line ashore
Anchor in the middle on a long scope
Bow line to a tree, no anchor at all
questions.why: In a narrow cove, anchor and take a stern line ashore so the boat cannot swing.

questions.q: Leaving the anchorage, your crew start the windlass. How do you help them?
options: Motor hard ahead to break it out first
Motor gently towards the anchor as they signal
Let the windlass pull the boat up to it
Motor astern to keep the chain tight
questions.why: Motor slowly up to the chain as the crew point; a windlass is not built to haul the boat.

questions.q: Leaving a lazy-line berth, how do you handle the lazy line?
options: Lead it aft and hand it to the quay
Keep it aboard until clear of the berth
Drop it at the bow and let it sink first
Drop it over the stern as you go ahead
questions.why: Let the lazy line sink clear before you motor ahead, or it can wrap round the propeller.

questions.q: You wake to find this. What do you do?

figure.title: Stern-to, 03:00
lines: Wind has swung onto the quay, F5
Stern now 0.5 m from the stone

options: Tighten the stern lines to hold her in
Ease the chain so she can ride it out
Add a fender and leave the lines alone
Tighten the chain and ease the stern lines
questions.why: Bring in chain to pull the stern off the quay, easing the stern lines to match.

questions.q: Where do you anchor?

figure.note: You carry 50 m of chain, draft 1.9 m

options: B — about 6 m of water
A — about 25 m of water
C — about 2.2 m of water
A — well clear of the beach
questions.why: 50 m of chain gives only 2:1 in 25 m; 2.2 m leaves no margin under a 1.9 m keel.

questions.q: You are going stern-to with a fresh wind blowing across the line of berths. Where do you drop the anchor?
options: A little downwind of the line of your berth
A little upwind of the line of your berth
Exactly in line, then reverse in harder
Close in, so the wind has less effect
questions.why: The wind will sag the boat downwind, leaving the chain running straight out from your berth.

questions.q: Where do you spend the night?

figure.title: Choosing tonight's cove
lines: Cove A: open to the south
Cove B: open to the north

options: A — it is sheltered from the wind now
A — the southerly will hold you off
B — sheltered from the stronger southerly
Either — any anchor holds in F5
questions.why: Pick shelter from the strongest forecast wind, not just the wind blowing now.

questions.q: What is the least chain you let out?
options: About 28 m
About 24 m
About 16 m
About 32 m
questions.why: Measure from the bow roller: (7 m + 1 m) × 4 = 32 m.

questions.q: You are about to hoist the mainsail outside the harbour. How do you point the boat?
options: Head to wind, motoring slowly
Downwind, so the sail fills at once
Straight for the next harbour
Beam-on, so the boat sits steady
questions.why: Head to wind the sail cannot fill, so it slides up without snagging.

questions.q: When do you put in a reef?
options: Only if the crew start to feel ill
Now, before you leave the bay
Once the wind actually reaches F5
When the boat starts to round up
questions.why: Reef when you first think of it — it is easy in calm water and hard in a blow.

questions.q: Your crew pull the sheet to unfurl the genoa. What do you do with the furling line?
options: Pull it in to help the sail unroll
Let it go so it runs out freely
Let it out under control, a turn on a winch
Keep it cleated until the sail is out
questions.why: Ease the furling line under control so the sail unrolls evenly and the line does not tangle.

questions.q: You roll the genoa away for the night in harbour. What do you check?
options: The furling line left uncleated
One sheet winched tight to hold it
A corner left out so the sail dries
Rolled tight, sheets wrapped twice round
questions.why: A tightly furled sail with the sheets wrapped round cannot unroll in a night gust.

questions.q: Reefing the main, you have eased the halyard and hooked the luff cringle on the reefing horn. What next?
options: Tension the halyard, then pull in the reef line
Sheet the main in hard, then the halyard
Tie in the reef points, then the halyard
Lower the whole sail down to the boom
questions.why: Slab reefing: tack down, halyard up tight, then the clew reef line, then the reef points.

questions.q: You are about to reef the main. What do you ease before letting the halyard down?
options: Nothing — let the halyard straight off
The mainsheet and the kicker
The genoa sheet and furling line
The outhaul and the backstay
questions.why: Easing the mainsheet and kicker spills the wind so the sail comes down freely.

questions.q: To reef your in-mast furling main, how do you work the two lines?
options: Lower the halyard a little, then wind in
Let the outhaul run free, then wind in fast
Ease the outhaul under control as you wind in
Wind in with the outhaul cleated tight
questions.why: Keep some tension on the outhaul as you furl so the sail rolls in tight and does not jam.

questions.q: What do you adjust?

figure.title: Genoa rolled to half
lines: Foot of the sail stretched tight

options: Move the sheet car aft
Unroll some genoa again
Ease the sheet out further
Move the sheet car forward
questions.why: A reefed genoa needs its sheet lead further forward to close the leech and ease the foot.

questions.q: You want to stop for a while at sea to clear a jammed line. How do you heave-to?
options: Tack, keep the genoa backed, helm lashed to luff
Tack, free the genoa, helm lashed to bear away
Gybe, keep the genoa backed, helm amidships
Drop both sails, helm lashed amidships
questions.why: Hove-to, the backed genoa pushes the bow off and the helm luffs it up, so she lies quietly.

questions.q: You call "Ready about". The crew on the genoa winch is still pulling on a jumper and says nothing. What do you do?
options: Gybe instead — it needs less crew
Wait for their "Ready" before you turn
Tack anyway — they will catch up
Call "Lee-oh" louder and turn
questions.why: As skipper you turn only when every crew member has answered "Ready".

questions.q: You are about to gybe in F4. What do you do with the mainsheet?
options: Let it run so the boom swings free
Free the kicker so the boom can lift
Sheet it in to the centre, then ease after
Leave it cleated and turn quickly
questions.why: Centring the boom before the gybe keeps its swing short and controlled.

questions.q: The boom keeps lifting and threatening to gybe. What do you rig?
options: A tighter topping lift to hold it up
A line from the boom to the mast foot
A line from the boom to the stern cleat
A preventer from the boom end to the bow
questions.why: A preventer led from the boom end forward to the bow holds the boom against an accidental gybe.

questions.q: Tacking about 45° either side of the wind, roughly how far do you sail?
options: About 14 miles
About 10 miles
About 28 miles
About 20 miles
questions.why: Each leg runs 45° off the direct line, so the distance is about 10 × 1.4 = 14 miles.

questions.q: Can you sail straight there?

figure.title: Next harbour
lines: The boat sails about 45° to the wind

options: Yes — on a close reach
No — it lies in the no-go zone
Yes — close-hauled on port tack
Yes — close-hauled on starboard tack
questions.why: The harbour is only 30° off the wind, inside the no-go zone; you must tack.

questions.q: Each gust heels the boat hard and she starts to round up. What is the quickest fix?
options: Pull the traveller up to windward
Bear away with the sheets still in
Drop the traveller to leeward in the gusts
Sheet the genoa in harder
questions.why: Easing the traveller or mainsheet spills wind from the main and stops her rounding up.

questions.q: Close-hauled, the windward telltales on your genoa are lifting and fluttering. What do you do?
options: Ease the sheet or luff up
Sheet in a little or luff up
Ease the sheet or bear away
Sheet in a little or bear away
questions.why: Fluttering windward telltales mean the luff is lifting: sheet in or bear away.

questions.q: Hoisting the main head to wind, the halyard suddenly gets very hard to winch halfway up. What do you do?
options: Stop and look up — something is caught
Use the electric winch to force it up
Keep winching — it always gets harder
Bear away so the wind lifts the sail
questions.why: A sudden hard hoist means a batten, lazy jack or reef line is caught; look before you pull.

questions.q: What is the safest way round?
options: Let the boom swing across on its own
Tack round through the wind instead
Gybe with the preventer still rigged
Gybe fast with the main eased right out
questions.why: In strong wind with a new crew, turning through the wind avoids a violent gybe.

questions.q: What do you do before you turn for the harbour?

figure.title: Morning run
lines: Running at 6 knots before the wind
On deck it feels like a light breeze

options: Shake out a reef for more power
Nothing — the wind has not changed
Reef — upwind it will feel much stronger
Ease all the sheets right out first
questions.why: Running, your speed cancels part of the wind; turn upwind and the apparent wind jumps.

questions.q: Which change helps most?

figure.title: Close-hauled, F5
lines: Full main, genoa rolled to two-thirds

options: Steer harder and carry on
Pull the traveller to windward
Roll away more genoa
Reef the main
questions.why: Too much mainsail makes her round up; reefing the main balances the helm.

questions.q: You are following the flotilla lead boat across to Kalamos. Your crew say, "Just follow them — they keep watch." What does Rule 5 require?
options: You keep your own lookout at all times
A lookout only in poor visibility
The AIS alarm counts as a lookout
The lead boat keeps lookout for all
questions.why: Rule 5: every vessel keeps a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times.

questions.q: Motoring across the Saronic Gulf, you take a compass bearing of a ferry: 040°, and again 040° five minutes later, and she is closer. What does it mean?
options: She is stopped in the water
Risk of collision exists
She will pass safely astern
She will pass safely ahead
questions.why: Rule 7: a steady compass bearing with the range closing means risk of collision.

questions.q: You are the give-way boat in a crossing with a motor yacht a mile off. How do you alter course?
options: At the last moment, to keep options open
A few degrees at a time, gradually
Early and boldly, so she clearly sees it
A little, then speed up to cross ahead
questions.why: Rule 8: action is early, large enough to be obvious, and leaves a safe distance.

questions.q: You are motoring through the narrow Lefkas canal and a tripper boat is coming the other way. Where do you keep?
options: To the port side, facing the traffic
In the middle, where it is deepest
Either side, as long as you go slowly
To the starboard side of the channel
questions.why: Rule 9: keep as near the starboard edge of a narrow channel as is safe.

questions.q: Sailing through the narrow strait at Poros, you meet this ferry. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Narrow channel · she can only use the channel

options: You — do not impede her in the channel
She does — she can stop more easily
Neither — both hold course and speed
She does — power gives way to sail
questions.why: Rule 9(b): a sailing vessel must not impede a vessel that can only navigate in the channel.

questions.q: Both yachts are under sail and converging. Who keeps clear?
options: Neither — both alter to starboard
You — you are on port tack
She does — she is on port tack
Whichever boat is to windward
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(i): on different tacks, the port-tack boat keeps clear.

questions.q: Under sail, you are converging with this yacht. Who keeps clear?
options: You do — you are to leeward
You do — she is on your starboard side
She does — she is to windward
Neither — same tack, both hold on
questions.why: Rule 12(a)(ii): on the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear of the leeward one.

questions.q: You are motoring at night and see these lights. What do you do?
options: Alter to port, passing starboard to starboard
Hold course — she must keep clear of you
Stop and wait for her to go past
Alter to starboard — she is head-on
questions.why: Rule 14: a masthead light and both sidelights dead ahead mean head-on; both turn to starboard.

questions.q: You are motoring. What do you do?
options: Hold your course and speed
Slow right down and let her pass ahead
Alter to starboard and pass astern
Alter to port and pass ahead of her
questions.why: Rule 15: she has you on her starboard side, so she gives way; you stand on (Rule 17).

questions.q: You are motoring and should stand on, but this yacht is not giving way. What do you do?

figure.note: She has not altered · now close

options: Hold on regardless — the rules protect you
Sound five short blasts and be ready to act
Speed up to get across ahead of her
Turn hard to port across her bow
questions.why: Rules 17 and 34(d): signal doubt, then act yourself — but not by turning to port for her.

questions.q: Sailing off Preveza, you are converging with a boat showing this shape. Who keeps clear?
options: She does — she is on your starboard side
She does — power gives way to sail
You — she is engaged in fishing
Neither — she is at anchor
questions.why: Rule 18: a sailing vessel keeps clear of a vessel engaged in fishing.

questions.q: You see this yacht with her sails up and this shape hoisted forward. What does it tell you?
options: She is fishing with nets
She is at anchor
She cannot manoeuvre easily
She is motoring as well as sailing
questions.why: Rule 25(e): a cone point down shows a yacht under sail and power — treat her as power.

questions.q: This yacht is under sail only. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Your engine is running, in gear

options: You — motor-sailing, you count as power
Neither — both of you have sails up
She does — she is on port tack
She does — she is on your port side
questions.why: Rule 3: with the engine in gear you are power-driven, so you keep clear of sail (Rule 18).

questions.q: Under sail alone, a motor yacht crosses from your starboard side on a steady bearing. Your crew say she has right of way because she is on your starboard side. Who keeps clear?
options: You do — she is on your starboard side
She does — power gives way to sail
You do — she is bigger and faster
Both alter course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 18: power keeps clear of sail; the starboard-side rule is for two power vessels.

questions.q: You are motoring at night with the sails stowed. Your yacht has a masthead tricolour, a steaming light on the mast and navigation lights at bow and stern. What do you switch on?
options: Sidelights and sternlight only
The tricolour and the steaming light
Steaming light, sidelights and sternlight
The masthead tricolour only
questions.why: Rule 23: under power you show a masthead (steaming) light, sidelights and a sternlight.

questions.q: You are motoring at night and see this single light high up. What is it, and what do you do?
options: A starboard-hand buoy — leave it to starboard
A power boat — you stand on
A yacht at anchor — pass either side
A yacht under sail — you keep clear
questions.why: A lone light high on a mast is a tricolour: a yacht under sail, so you, under power, keep clear.

questions.q: In Poros harbour, a ferry near the quay sounds three short blasts. What does she mean?
options: I am operating astern propulsion
I doubt that you are keeping clear
I am altering my course to port
I am altering my course to starboard
questions.why: Rule 34(a): one short = to starboard, two = to port, three = astern propulsion.

questions.q: In fog off the Croatian coast you hear one prolonged blast about every two minutes, getting closer. What is it?
options: A sailing vessel under way
A power-driven vessel making way
A vessel at anchor
A vessel aground
questions.why: Rule 35(a): a power vessel making way sounds one prolonged blast at least every 2 minutes.

questions.q: You are catching up this yacht from astern. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You are faster, closing from astern

options: Whichever of you is the larger
She does — she is on port tack
You — you are overtaking her
Neither — both hold course and speed
questions.why: Rule 13 overrides Rule 12: an overtaking vessel keeps clear, whatever the tacks.

questions.q: Crossing to Paxos at night under engine, you watch these lights for five minutes. What do you do?

figure.note: Night · on your starboard bow, bearing steady

options: Turn to port and pass ahead of her
Stand on — she must turn to starboard
Speed up and cross ahead of her
Give way — turn to starboard, pass astern
questions.why: Her red sidelight shows her port side: she is crossing from your starboard, so you give way.

questions.q: Entering Argostoli from the sea, you pass this buoy. On which side do you leave it?
options: On your port side
Close on its seaward side
On your starboard side
On either side
questions.why: Region A: a red can marks the port side of the channel going in.

questions.q: You see this mark off a headland. Where is the safe water?
options: All around it
To the north of it
To the east of it
To the south of it
questions.why: North cardinal: both cones point up; pass to the north of it.

questions.q: Approaching Lefkas at night, you see a white light: six quick flashes, then one long flash. Where do you pass the mark?
options: To the east of it
To the west of it
To the south of it
To the north of it
questions.why: Q(6)+LFl is a south cardinal; the long flash tells it apart from Q(3) and Q(9).

questions.q: Your planned track passes 100 m west of this mark. Is that safe?
options: Yes — west is its safe side
No — pass on its north side
Yes — 100 m is enough either side
No — pass on its east side
questions.why: East cardinal: cones base to base, light Q(3); the safe water is to the east.

questions.q: Your pilot book says this mark guards a reef. Where is the reef?
options: To the east of the mark
To the north of the mark
Right underneath the mark
To the west of the mark
questions.why: West cardinal: the safe water is to the west, so the danger lies to the east.

questions.q: Off a point near Sivota you see this mark. How do you pass it?
options: Close by — it marks deep water
Either side, giving it a good berth
Leave it to port, like a lateral
Only to its north, like a cardinal
questions.why: Isolated danger: a small danger with navigable water all round — keep well off.

questions.q: Approaching a harbour, you find this mark ahead. What does it tell you?
options: A danger — keep well clear
A swimming area — keep out
Safe water all round it
The port side of the channel
questions.why: Safe water mark: red and white stripes, a red ball; it often marks a fairway or landfall.

questions.q: Off a beach near Kos you see a line of these. What are they?

figure.note: One of a line off the beach

options: Lateral marks — keep them to starboard
Safe water marks — sail between them
Cardinal marks — pass to their north
Special marks — check the chart
questions.why: Yellow with an X: a special mark, often a bathing area limit; the chart says which.

questions.q: The pilot book gives the harbour entrance light as Fl(2) R 6s. What will you see?
options: Two red flashes every 6 seconds
Six red flashes, then 2 s dark
A red flash every 2 seconds
Two red flashes, each 6 seconds long
questions.why: Fl(2) = groups of two flashes; R = red; 6s = the whole cycle repeats every 6 seconds.

questions.q: At a harbour entrance you time a white light: on for 3 seconds, off for 1, repeating. How is it shown on the chart?
options: LFl 4s — one long flash
Oc 4s — light longer than dark
Fl 4s — light shorter than dark
Iso 4s — light and dark equal
questions.why: Occulting: the light is on longer than it is off; the period is 3 + 1 = 4 s.

questions.q: Entering an unfamiliar harbour at night, you see these lights on the pierheads. Where do you steer?
options: Leave both lights on your starboard side
Head for the red light, then turn
Between them: red to port, green to starboard
Leave both lights on your port side
questions.why: Region A: the red light marks the port side going in, the green the starboard side.

questions.q: Next year you charter in the Caribbean, in IALA region B. Entering harbour from sea, on which side do you leave a red lateral mark?
options: On your port side, as in the Med
On the side away from the land
On either side — it marks a danger
On your starboard side
questions.why: Region B (the Americas) reverses the colours: red is left to starboard going in.

questions.q: In a channel between two islands, you meet this mark. On which side do you leave it?

figure.note: Buoyage direction: north · you head south

options: On your port side
Close on its east side
On your starboard side
On either side
questions.why: Lateral marks follow the direction of buoyage; heading against it, a green cone goes to port.

questions.q: At night you count nine quick white flashes, then darkness, repeating. On which side of the mark is the safe water?
options: To the south of it
To the west of it
To the east of it
All around it
questions.why: Q(9) or VQ(9) is a west cardinal: think of nine o'clock on a clock face.

questions.q: How do you pass this mark?
options: Alter to starboard, leaving it to port
Hold course and pass close alongside
Alter to port, leaving it to starboard
Turn back — the danger lies beyond it
questions.why: Pass north of a north cardinal: heading east, north is to port, so the mark stays to starboard.

questions.q: On the chart, a buoy's light is shown just as "Q" — no colour letter. What do you look for at night?
options: A red light flashing quickly, non-stop
A white light, one long flash every 10 s
A yellow light flashing quickly, non-stop
A white light flashing quickly, non-stop
questions.why: No colour letter means white; Q alone is continuous quick flashing — a north cardinal.

questions.q: Entering the channel at night, you find this light close on your starboard bow. What does it tell you?
options: You are on the wrong side — keep it to port
It is a starboard mark — keep it there
Fine — leave it to starboard as you pass
It is an isolated danger — pass either side
questions.why: Going in, a red light is left to port; having it to starboard puts you outside the channel.

questions.q: Your planned track runs between these two marks. Is it safe?
options: Yes — cardinals mark the channel edges
No — the danger lies between them
Only by day, with both marks in sight
Yes — keep exactly halfway between
questions.why: A north cardinal lies north of a danger and a south cardinal south of it, so the danger is between.

questions.q: Leaving Gouvia marina for the open sea at night, you see a flashing red light ahead, low on the water. On which side do you leave it?
options: Steer straight for it
On your port side
On your starboard side
On either side, 50 m off
questions.why: Heading out to sea the lateral rule reverses: red marks stay on your starboard side.

questions.q: Coming in on the safe white sector of this light, you see it change. What does it mean?
options: The red sector is the deepest water
You are closer — red means nearly in
The light is faulty — ignore it
You have left the safe sector — check the chart
questions.why: A sector light shows white over the safe approach; a coloured sector means you are off the line.

questions.q: You are planning a short cut across the bay. One figure on the chart is underlined. What does it tell you?

figure.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

options: A rock or bank dries 1.2 m above datum
There is 12 m of water — the line is a decimal
There is 1.2 m more water than the chart shows
There is 1.2 m of water over it at datum
questions.why: An underlined sounding is a drying height: it stands that much above chart datum. Keep well clear.

questions.q: You have drawn today's leg on the paper chart and spanned it with dividers. Where do you read off the distance in miles?
options: On the outer ring of the compass rose
On the latitude scale at the side, level with the leg
On the longitude scale along the top or bottom
On the kilometre scale bar under the title
questions.why: One minute of latitude is one nautical mile; minutes of longitude shrink as you go north.

questions.q: You have a 1:50 000 chart of the area and a 1:10 000 harbour plan in the pilot book. Which do you use to pick your way into the harbour?
options: Either — same detail, only drawn at another size
Neither — only the plotter shows harbour detail
The 1:10 000 plan — larger scale, more detail
The 1:50 000 chart — bigger number, more detail
questions.why: 1:10 000 is a larger scale than 1:50 000: a smaller area drawn in more detail.

questions.q: You are coming in to this town quay to berth stern-to. Which spot do you ask for?

figure.note: Depths in metres alongside the quay

options: A — the root of the quay is most sheltered
Any — depths on a plan are only a guide
B — 2.0 m, the tide will add the rest
C — 4.0 m leaves water under the keel
questions.why: Pick a berth deeper than your draft, with a margin; the Med tide adds almost nothing.

questions.q: You want a swim stop before the afternoon leg. What is the latest time you can leave the swim stop?

figure.title: Lead crew briefing
lines: Your speed under engine: about 6 kn
Be in by 17:00 — keep an hour in hand

questions.why: 12 M at 6 kn takes 2 hours; with an hour in hand you arrive at 16:00, so leave by 14:00.

questions.q: The lead crew wants every boat at the lunch stop, 14 miles away, by 13:00. You leave at 09:30. What average speed do you need?
options: 5 knots
4 knots
4.5 knots
3.5 knots
questions.why: 09:30 to 13:00 is 3.5 hours; 14 M ÷ 3.5 h = 4 knots.

questions.q: You have drawn the course to the next headland on the chart. What do you steer by the compass?
questions.why: True to magnetic: subtract easterly variation — 140° − 4° = 136°.

questions.q: You take this bearing of a lighthouse with the hand-bearing compass. Which true bearing do you draw on the chart?
questions.why: Magnetic to true: add easterly variation — 030° + 5° = 035°.

questions.q: You are entering harbour on a leading line. The rear beacon has moved a little to the right of the front one. What do you do?
options: Alter to port until they are in line again
Alter to starboard until they are in line again
Steer straight for the rear beacon instead
Hold course — they will line up as you close
questions.why: Rear mark open to the right of the front means you are right of the line: come back to port.

questions.q: The pilot book says: 'Enter with the chapel in line with the white house, 320°.' Why follow the transit rather than steer 320° on the compass?
options: It is only needed when the compass has failed
It shows at once if wind or current set you off
It also tells you how far off the entrance you are
It still works when the visibility closes in
questions.why: A transit is a line on the ground: if the marks open, you are off it, whatever your heading.

questions.q: You plan to spend the night at anchor here. How much water do you plan on?

figure.title: Ionian anchorage
lines: Pilot book: tidal range about 0.3 m

options: About 1.5 m — half the charted depth at low water
About 6 m — double the charted depth at high water
About 3 m — the charted depth, give or take a little
Under 1.9 m — you will touch at low water
questions.why: Med tides are tiny and chart datum is near the lowest level, so the charted depth is about what you get.

questions.q: You are motoring along the coast in clear weather. What do you make of this?

figure.title: Plotter vs. what you see
lines: Plotter: your boat drawn on the land
Headland about 300 m off to port

options: The GPS has lost its fix — stop the boat at once
The sounder is faulty — the plotter is always right
The headland is nearer than it looks — trust the plotter
The chart on the plotter is offset — trust your eyes
questions.why: Electronic charts can be offset by tens or hundreds of metres; what you see and the sounder come first.

questions.q: Today's route takes you through a narrow pass between an island and a reef. The plotter is working well. How do you take the pass?
options: Follow the plotter, checking it against marks and depth
Zoom the plotter right in and follow its line exactly
Engage the autopilot on the plotter's route
Trust the GPS alone — it is accurate to a few metres
questions.why: The GPS is good, but the chart under it may not be: confirm with transits, bearings and the sounder.

questions.q: You are at anchor at 38°31'N. The next anchorage is due north at 38°43'N. How long does it take at 6 knots?
options: 3 hours
2 hours
12 minutes
1 hour 12 minutes
questions.why: 12 minutes of latitude = 12 M; 12 M ÷ 6 kn = 2 hours.

questions.q: You check the route you drew for this afternoon against the chart. What do you do?
options: Go as drawn — 1.8 m is near enough your draft
Go as drawn, but slow down over the patch
Redraw the leg to pass clear of the 1.8 m patch
Go as drawn — the tide will give you more water
questions.why: The track crosses a sounding shallower than your draft; plan every leg clear of it with a margin.

questions.q: You enter the lead crew's lunch-stop waypoint into the plotter and press 'Go to'. What must you do before following the line?
options: Check only that the waypoint name is right
Set the autopilot first so you hold the line
Nothing — the plotter steers round any danger
Check the straight line on the chart for land and shoals
questions.why: 'Go to' draws a straight line, and it will cross headlands, rocks and shallows if they are in the way.

questions.q: You are motoring along this coast toward the headland. The pilot book gives the clearing bearing shown. What do you do?
options: Turn offshore until the bearing drops below 070°
Turn inshore until the bearing reads 070°
Hold course and check again at the headland
Hold on — over 070° means you are well clear
questions.why: 078° is on the wrong side of the clearing line, toward the rocks: turn away until it is below 070°.

questions.q: When do you expect to arrive in the evening harbour?

figure.title: Today's plan
lines: Leg 1: 9 M at 6 kn to the lunch bay
Leg 2: 6 M at 4 kn under sail

questions.q: You are motoring in exactly on the leading line from the pilot book. What does the steering compass tell you?
options: It reads 5° low — have it checked
You are 5° off the line — alter course
It is right — 312° true is 307° magnetic
The pilot book's line is 5° wrong
questions.why: Easterly variation is subtracted: 312° − 5° = 307°M, so the compass has no deviation on this heading.

questions.q: You want to put your position on the paper chart. What latitude do you plot?
Tomorrow's forecast for your area is northwest force 7. What does that mean for your 12 m charter yacht?
options: Near gale, 28–33 kn — stay in harbour
Strong breeze, 22–27 kn — two reefs
Fresh breeze, 17–21 kn — one reef
Moderate breeze, 11–16 kn — full sail
questions.why: Force 7 is a near gale, 28–33 knots: more than a flotilla boat should go out in.

questions.q: Your flotilla is in the Cyclades in August and the lead crew warns of the Meltemi. Where will it blow from?
options: From the east
From the north
From the west
From the south
questions.why: The Meltemi is the Aegean's summer northerly: NE in the north, N in the Cyclades, NW in the Dodecanese.

questions.q: This is tomorrow's forecast chart, and you are where the boat is drawn. What wind do you expect?
options: Light wind — close isobars mean a calm area
Light wind — you are near the centre of the low
Strong wind — the isobars are packed close
No change — isobars show pressure, not wind
questions.why: The closer together the isobars, the stronger the wind.

questions.q: You are in a remote Ionian anchorage with no phone signal. How do you get tomorrow's official forecast?
options: Use yesterday's forecast — it covers three days
Read the barometer and the clouds — that is enough
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for it
Listen to the coast station's VHF broadcasts or read NAVTEX
questions.why: Coast stations broadcast forecasts and warnings on VHF at set times; NAVTEX prints them aboard.

questions.q: You must make this leg today. When do you go?

figure.title: Meltemi forecast
lines: Your leg: 15 M north to the next island

options: At first light, to arrive before midday
In the late afternoon, when the peak has passed
After lunch, once the wind has settled
At midday, when the morning breeze has gone
questions.why: The Meltemi is usually lightest in the early morning and strongest in the afternoon.

questions.q: Your crew hopes it will blow itself out overnight. How do you plan?

figure.title: Cyclades, late July
lines: Forecast: the same for 3 more days

options: Go at dawn — it always dies after one day
Expect it to last — sheltered legs only, or stay put
Go tomorrow afternoon, once it has peaked
Go now — it will only get worse later
questions.why: A Meltemi often blows for days: plan on the forecast, not on hope, and ask the lead crew for a sheltered route.

questions.q: It is a calm, sunny July morning in the Ionian. What wind do you plan on for the afternoon?
options: Calm all day — sunny days bring no wind
A south wind, building through the night
A northwest breeze, building to about force 4
A gale — a calm morning comes before a storm
questions.why: In summer the Ionian's northwesterly builds from late morning and dies away around sunset.

questions.q: You are anchored off a beach on a hot, settled day. In the early afternoon a breeze sets in from the sea. What does it mean for you?
options: It will die within minutes — sea breezes are brief
It blows offshore — the beach gives you shelter
A front is coming — expect rain by evening
It blows onshore — the beach is now a lee shore
questions.why: On hot days the sea breeze blows from sea to land, putting boats off a beach on a lee shore until evening.

questions.q: You are choosing where to anchor for the night in this bay. Where do you go?

figure.note: Pilot book: violent gusts down the valley at night

options: B — well clear of the valley mouth
Mid-bay, as far from the land as you can
Either — the gusts hit the whole bay equally
A — right off the valley, closest to the beach
questions.why: At night gusts pour down valleys off high land; anchor away from the valley mouth.

questions.q: The cloud will reach you before you reach harbour. What do you do with the sails now?

figure.title: Late afternoon, August
lines: Tall dark cloud building over the mainland
Thunder heard, the cloud is coming your way
4 M to harbour, full sail set

options: Head out to sea, away from the lightning
Reef or drop sail now, before the squall arrives
Wait for the first gust, then decide
Keep full sail and race the cloud to harbour
questions.why: Thunderstorms bring sudden violent squalls; reduce sail before they hit, not during.

questions.q: You are anchored here for the night. What does the forecast mean for you?
options: Nothing — veering changes only the wind's strength
It falls calm — veering means the wind dies away
The wind swings into the open west — move before dark
The wind swings to the east — better shelter still
questions.why: Veering is a clockwise shift: south to west turns this bay into a lee shore.

questions.q: You are in harbour planning tomorrow's leg. What do these readings suggest?

figure.title: Barometer log
lines: Sky: high cloud thickening from the west

options: A normal daily swing — nothing to note
A high is building — settled weather to come
The wind will drop — a falling glass means calm
A low is approaching — expect the wind to rise
questions.why: A steady fall of 1 hPa an hour with thickening cloud points to a low and stronger wind.

questions.q: You read the wind instrument before slipping your lines. How do you set up the boat?

figure.title: Wind instrument at the quay
lines: Your leg: 12 M on a beam reach
Crew: two who have sailed before

options: Force 5 — take in a reef before you go
Force 9 — stay in and double the lines
Force 3 — shake out every reef, full sail
Force 7 — stay in harbour, a near gale
questions.why: 18 kn mean is force 5 (17–21 kn); reef in harbour, not out in the gusts.

questions.q: Tomorrow's chart puts you here, under this pattern. What do you plan for the day?
options: Strong winds — reef before you leave
Light winds — plan to motor part of the way
A gale — stay in harbour all day
Thunderstorms — a high always brings them
questions.why: Widely spaced isobars round a high mean light winds; allow time and fuel for motoring.

questions.q: You are deciding whether to sail today. What do you choose?
options: Leave now under full sail to beat the rise
Leave at midday, once the wind has peaked
Stay in harbour — it is too much for this crew
Leave now and reef only when it reaches 7
questions.why: 14 M upwind takes over four hours, into force 6–7 with a new crew: the safe call is to stay.

questions.q: The forecast reads: 'Northwest 4 to 5, locally 6.' Your route rounds a high cape and goes through a channel between islands. What do you expect there?
options: Force 6 for a few minutes in every hour
Force 6 only at night, when the land cools
Force 6 only far offshore, out of sight of land
Force 6 in places — round capes and in channels
questions.why: 'Locally' means stronger in places — typically where the wind is squeezed round capes and between islands.

questions.q: The marine forecast gives 'wind 15 knots, gusts 25 knots' for your afternoon leg. What do you set your sails for?
options: The 25 kn gusts, not the 15 kn mean
The 15 kn mean — gusts pass quickly
A reef for 15 kn, shaken out in the gusts
Full sail — gusts are only felt at anchor
questions.why: Your sail plan must cope with the gusts, and 25 kn is already force 6.

questions.q: You are sailing with the VHF on channel 16 and hear a SÉCURITÉ call announcing a gale warning on another channel. What do you do?
options: Wait for the full warning to be read on 16
Switch to the channel given and listen to the warning
Ignore it — gale warnings are for ships
Reply on 16 to confirm you have heard it
questions.why: SÉCURITÉ is announced on 16 and read out on a working channel: switch over, listen, then go back to 16.

questions.q: Your crew prefers the phone app. Which forecast do you plan on?

figure.title: Two forecasts for tomorrow
lines: NAVTEX: warning, NW 7 in your area

options: The app, unless the barometer starts to fall
The app — it is more detailed for your spot
The official one — plan for force 6–7
An average of the two — plan for force 5
questions.why: Plan on the official forecast and warnings, and on the worse of two forecasts that disagree.

questions.q: Your crew says nothing can blow from a sky like this. Are they right?

figure.title: Paros, early August
lines: Sky clear blue, not a cloud

options: Only if the barometer starts to fall later
Yes — a steady barometer means light winds
Yes — strong wind always comes with cloud
No — the Meltemi blows hard under clear skies
questions.why: The Meltemi is a fair-weather wind: clear sky, steady barometer, and still force 6–7.

questions.q: It is your first morning on the charter yacht. What do you check before you start the engine?
options: Oil, coolant, belt and the raw-water strainer
Fuel gauge only — the base checks the rest
Gearbox oil and the shaft anode only
Battery water and the spark plug leads
questions.why: Daily check: oil and coolant levels, belt tension, strainer clear, bilge dry, fuel on.

questions.q: At the fuel quay the attendant reaches for the nozzle marked 'Unleaded 95'. What do you do?
options: Let him, then add a bottle of additive
Stop him — the engine takes diesel only
Let him if the tank is half full of diesel
Let him — any fuel will do for one fill
questions.why: Yacht engines are diesels; petrol in the tank means draining it, with a fire risk and engine damage.

questions.q: You have just started the engine. What do you check at the stern before casting off?
options: Bubbles rising from the propeller
A thin film of oil on the water astern
Cooling water spurting out with the exhaust
Black smoke coming out with the exhaust
questions.why: No water from the exhaust means no cooling flow: stop the engine and check the seacock and strainer.

questions.q: You are settling in for the evening at anchor. Which battery do you run the boat from?

lines: Fridge, lights and music to run

options: Whichever one shows the higher voltage
Both together, so they share the load evenly
The engine battery, saving the house one for the night
The house battery, keeping the engine one for starting
questions.why: Domestic loads run from the house bank; the engine battery stays isolated so you can always start.

questions.q: You are motoring in open water, well clear of other boats, when this happens. What do you do?
options: Stop the engine, then check the cooling water intake
Carry on — the harbour is only 2 miles away
Open the coolant cap at once to top it up
Raise the revs to pump more water through
questions.why: Overheating with little exhaust water means the raw-water flow has failed: stop before the engine is damaged.

questions.q: This alarm goes off as you motor across the bay. What do you do?

lines: Oil pressure alarm and warning light

options: Carry on at low revs to the next harbour
Stop the engine at once and check the oil level
Top up the coolant, then carry on
Ignore it — the temperature is normal
questions.why: Low oil pressure can wreck a diesel within minutes; stop it and find out why.

questions.q: You are going to clean the strainer. What is the right order?

figure.title: Raw-water strainer
lines: Strainer bowl packed with sea grass

options: Open the strainer lid with the seacock left open
Clean it, then leave the seacock shut to be safe
Close the seacock, clean the strainer, open the seacock
Clean it with the engine running to flush it
questions.why: Close the seacock first or the sea pours in; reopen it before starting or the engine overheats again.

questions.q: How much fuel will be left when you arrive?

lines: Today's leg: 30 M under engine, calm
Keep at least 15 L in reserve

options: 10 litres — below the reserve
20 litres — just above the reserve
45 litres — well above the reserve
30 litres — well above the reserve
questions.why: 30 M ÷ 6 kn = 5 h; 5 h × 4 L/h = 20 L used; 50 − 20 = 30 L left.

questions.q: What do you do about the house battery?

lines: Second night at anchor, fridge on

options: Run the engine to charge it, or plug in to shore power
Switch to BOTH and leave it there overnight
Switch off the engine battery to save power
Nothing — 11.9 V means it is fully charged
questions.why: 11.9 V at rest is a well-flattened house bank; recharge it from the alternator or shore power.

questions.q: You arrive in a marina and want shore power. In what order do you connect the cable?
options: Either way — the cable is waterproof
Boat end first, then the shore pillar
Shore pillar first, then the boat end
Both ends at once, with the breaker on
questions.why: Plug in at the boat first so there is never a live loose end; unplug at the pillar first.

questions.q: Your crew is in the shower when this happens. What is wrong?

figure.title: Fresh water
lines: Pump runs and does not stop
Two tanks, selector set to tank 1

options: The pump fuse has blown — replace it
The water heater has an air lock — run the engine
Tank 1 is empty — switch off the pump, change tanks
The shower drain is blocked — clear it
questions.why: A pump that runs on while the taps spit air has emptied its tank; a pump running dry can burn out.

questions.q: You are moored stern-to in a busy town harbour. Where should the heads empty to?
options: Into the grey-water drain under the galley
Straight overboard — the harbour flushes it out
Into the bilge — the bilge pump clears it later
Into the holding tank, to be emptied well offshore
questions.why: In harbours and anchorages the heads go to the holding tank; empty it well out at sea or at a pump-out.

questions.q: Your crew has finished cooking pasta. How do they turn off the gas?
options: Solenoid off, let the flame die, then the burner knob
Burner knob off first, then the solenoid
Burner knob only — the solenoid stays on all week
Bottle valve only, the next morning
questions.why: Shutting the supply first lets the flame burn off the gas left in the pipe, so none sits in the line.

questions.q: You come below and smell gas in the saloon. What do you do?
options: Turn on the cabin fan to blow the gas out
Turn off the bottle, no switches or flames, air the boat
Run the electric bilge pump to clear it
Light the stove to burn off what is left
questions.why: Gas is heavier than air and any spark can ignite it: shut the supply, leave the switches alone, ventilate.

questions.q: The bilge is fuller than usual. The electric bilge pump is on AUTO but stays silent. What do you do?
options: Wait — on AUTO it will start by itself
Turn the battery switch off and on again
Pump by hand, then check the fuse and float switch
Run the engine — it pumps the bilge as it cools
questions.why: Use the manual pump to keep up, then look for a blown fuse or a jammed float switch.

questions.q: The engine note changes suddenly as you motor along. What has most likely happened?

figure.title: Motoring past fishing floats
lines: Speed drops, though the revs are the same

options: The gearbox has slipped into neutral
Air has got into the fuel system
The raw-water intake has blocked
A rope has wrapped round the propeller
questions.why: A thump, vibration and lost speed near floats point to a rope round the prop: neutral, and stop the engine.

questions.q: The engine is running, yet the battery is not charging. What is the likely cause?

lines: Engine running, charge warning light on
A squeal from the engine box at start-up

options: The alternator belt is slack or broken
The house battery is fully charged
The fuel filter is partly blocked
The shore power cable is still plugged in
questions.why: No charge plus a squealing belt means a slipping belt; on many engines it also drives the water pump.

questions.q: You turn the key to leave the anchorage. Why will the engine not start?

figure.title: Morning at anchor
lines: Battery switch left on BOTH all night
Starter clicks but will not turn the engine

options: The engine battery charges only from shore power
On BOTH the fridge drained the engine battery too
Overnight the fuel has drained back to the tank
The house battery is fine, so the starter has failed
questions.why: BOTH joins the banks, so domestic loads flatten the starting battery as well; keep it isolated.

questions.q: The overheat alarm goes off close to this rocky shore. What do you do first?

lines: Rocky shore 0.3 M downwind, F4 onshore

options: Stop the engine at once and drift while you check it
Keep motoring flat out to get clear quickly
Unroll the genoa and sail clear, then stop the engine
Go below and clear the strainer with it running
questions.why: The boat's safety first: get sea room under sail, then stop the engine before it is damaged.

questions.q: You have cleared the strainer, but the problem remains. What do you suspect, and what do you do?

figure.title: After clearing the strainer
lines: Engine restarted: still no water at the exhaust
Lead boat 3 M away, calm sea

options: A flat battery — switch to BOTH and restart
An empty fuel tank — refill and restart
A full holding tank — pump it out at sea
A failed impeller — stop and call the lead crew
questions.why: With the intake clear, no flow points to the raw-water pump impeller; the lead crew's engineer can change it.

questions.q: The base hands you the check-in sheet to sign. What do you do before you sign it?

figure.title: Check-in at the base
lines: Base staff walk round the boat with you
You find a deep scratch on the bow
It is not on the check-in sheet

options: Have it added to the check-in sheet
Sign — a scratch is too small to matter
Mention it at the evening briefing instead
Take a photo, but leave the sheet as it is
questions.why: Anything not on the check-in sheet may be charged to you at check-out.

questions.q: Your crew is aboard and you are about to leave the base for the first time. What do you do first?
options: Cast off — the base has briefed everyone already
Brief them on lifejackets, fire, MOB gear, liferaft and VHF
Explain the galley and the heads, then cast off
Hand out the drinks and brief them at lunch
questions.why: The skipper's safety briefing comes before the lines are let go: where the gear is and how to use it.

questions.q: The lead crew holds a briefing on the quay every morning. What do you take away from it?
options: Only the time of departure — you follow the others
Only the weather — the route is up to you
Route, weather, destination and the harbour plan
Nothing — the briefing is optional for skippers
questions.why: The morning briefing gives every skipper the day's route, forecast and berthing plan for the next harbour.

questions.q: It is the last afternoon and the charter agreement says to return the boat with a full tank. What do you do?
options: Return it with whatever is left and say nothing
Fill up only if the gauge reads under a quarter
Return it as it is — the base fills every boat free
Fill up at the fuel quay before going back to base
questions.why: Return the boat as agreed: with a full tank, or the base charges for the fuel, often at a high rate.

questions.q: Which of these do you report to the coastguard first, rather than to the lead crew?
options: A crew member unconscious after a fall
An engine that will not restart at anchor
A blocked toilet at the lunch stop
A torn genoa on a calm afternoon
questions.why: Danger to life goes to the coastguard first, then the lead crew; breakdowns go to the lead crew.

questions.q: The port police officer is waiting at your stern. Which documents do you hand over?

figure.title: Port police on the quay
lines: An officer asks for the skipper

options: Only the charter invoice and the deposit receipt
The boat's papers, the crew list and your certificate
Nothing — flotilla boats are exempt from checks
Only the passports — the boat is the base's affair
questions.why: The skipper carries the boat's papers, the crew list and a valid certificate for port authorities.

questions.q: You are moored stern-to on a busy town quay. Another boat is reversing into the gap beside you. What do you do?
options: Shout directions to them from your cockpit
Push them off with your feet if they come close
Put crew on that side with a fender, ready to take a line
Stay below — it is their skipper's job alone
questions.why: Good harbour manners: fend off and take your neighbour's lines; next time it will be you coming in.

questions.q: Your crew opens beers as you leave the lunch stop for a two-hour sail to the evening harbour. What is your rule?
options: Anything goes, as long as nobody is seasick
No rule — the lead boat watches the flotilla
A beer each is fine for everyone, skipper too
No alcohol for you or whoever helms until moored
questions.why: The skipper must stay fit to command and the helm alert; the drinks wait until you are safely moored.

questions.q: Your crew wants to visit a famous beach 25 miles outside the flotilla's sailing area. What do you say?
options: No — stay in the agreed area and ask the lead crew for ideas
Yes — and tell the lead crew when you get back
Yes — if you leave early and return by dark
Yes — the area is only a suggestion
questions.why: The flotilla's area is part of your charter terms and the lead crew's cover; you stay within it.

questions.q: Your crew asks you to take the boat out anyway. What is your answer?

figure.title: Morning briefing
lines: Lead crew: all boats stay in harbour today
Your crew is keen to go

options: Go if one other skipper agrees to come too
Stay in harbour with the rest of the flotilla
Go early and be back before the wind arrives
Go, but promise to call on the working channel
questions.why: Flotilla boats do not sail in conditions above the agreed limits; the lead crew's call stands.

questions.q: On day three you touch the quay while berthing and crack a stanchion base. When do you tell anyone?
options: Never — small damage is covered by the deposit
Only at check-out, if the base staff notice it
Tell the lead crew now, and list it at check-out
Only if it gets worse during the week
questions.why: Report damage at once: the lead crew can fix it, it may affect safety, and it goes on the return report.

questions.q: It is blowing force 5 and the sea is rough. One crew member refuses to wear a lifejacket on deck. What do you do?
options: Let them decide — they are an adult
Ask the lead crew to talk to them by radio
Let them, but keep them in the cockpit
Insist — on deck in these conditions, lifejackets are on
questions.why: The skipper is responsible for everyone aboard and decides on safety gear; the crew follow.

questions.q: You count the safety gear at check-in. What must be put right before you leave?
options: One more lifejacket — one for every person
Nothing — seven is enough for a coastal flotilla
The flares — they must be renewed every week
The liferaft — it needs a service first
questions.why: Every person aboard needs a lifejacket; count them at check-in, before you sign.

questions.q: The lead boat's 17:00 call comes through on the working channel. How do you reply?

figure.title: Flotilla radio schedule
lines: Lead boat calls all boats at 09:00 and 17:00
17:00 now: you are 5 M from the harbour

options: Answer only if something is wrong
Answer with your position and expected arrival
Call back later on channel 16 instead
Stay silent — you will be in within the hour
questions.why: The radio schedule is how the lead crew knows every boat is safe: always answer with position and ETA.

questions.q: Your fresh-water pump has failed at a remote anchorage, and the lead boat does not answer on the working channel. What do you do?
options: Send a PAN-PAN so that the lead boat hears it
Call the coastguard on channel 16 for advice
Phone the lead crew on the number from the briefing
Fire a flare to attract the lead boat
questions.why: A breakdown with no danger is for the lead crew; if the VHF does not reach, use their mobile number.

questions.q: During your safety briefing, who do you make sure can use the VHF and bring the boat back to a man overboard?
options: Nobody — the lead boat handles emergencies
Whoever is nearest, once something happens
Only you — the radio is the skipper's job
At least one other crew member besides you
questions.why: If the skipper is the one overboard or hurt, someone else must be able to call for help and handle the boat.

questions.q: The engine is dead but the boat sails well. How do you handle the rest of the leg?

figure.title: Afternoon leg
lines: Wind W 3, sailing well, sea calm

options: Sail on and call the lead crew to plan your arrival
Anchor here and wait for the base engineer
Send a MAYDAY on channel 16 at once
Sail on and say nothing until you arrive
questions.why: No danger, so no distress call; but the lead crew must know, to help you berth or tow you in.

questions.q: Late at night, after a long dinner ashore, your crew want to take the dinghy back to the boat at anchor. Two of them are drunk. What do you decide?
options: Let the drunkest drive — it is only 200 metres
A sober driver, lifejackets on, the drunk ones sitting low
Let them swim back — the water is warm
Everyone goes, no lifejackets — it is a calm night
questions.why: Night dinghy trips after drinking are a classic way to lose crew: sober driver, lifejackets, a torch.

questions.q: The lead boat calls on the radio schedule. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Lead crew: all boats in by 18:00

options: ETA about 19:00 — an hour late
ETA about 17:30 — in good time
ETA about 18:20 — slightly late
ETA about 18:00 — just in time
questions.why: 14 M ÷ 5 kn = 2.8 h, about 2 h 50: 15:30 + 2:50 ≈ 18:20. Say so, or motor-sail to make it up.

questions.q: Your flotilla is based in Kos. The crew wants to pop across to the Turkish coast, 4 miles away, for lunch at anchor. What do you say?
options: Yes — as long as you fly a Turkish courtesy flag
Yes — as long as nobody goes ashore
Yes — a lunch stop at anchor needs no papers
No — you would have to clear out of Greece and into Turkey
questions.why: Crossing a border means customs and immigration clearance both ways, and it is outside the flotilla's area.

questions.q: A crew member falls over the side while you are sailing. What are the first things you do?
options: Shout 'man overboard', throw the lifebuoy, keep pointing
Turn hard toward them at full speed
Start the engine and put it in gear at once
Go below and send a MAYDAY before anything else
questions.why: Raise the alarm, give them buoyancy, and never lose sight: one crew member does nothing but point.

questions.q: Which signal do you use to show them where you are?

figure.title: Daytime, engine dead, drifting
lines: Aboard: parachute rockets, red hand flares,

options: A red parachute rocket, fired straight up
Orange smoke, on the downwind side
A red hand flare, held up to windward
Nothing — wait until they are overhead
questions.why: In daylight orange smoke shows an aircraft your position and the wind; never fire a rocket near a helicopter.

questions.q: Your yacht is damaged and taking water, but it is still afloat. When do you get into the liferaft?
options: As soon as water comes in — the raft is safer
Once the lead boat is in sight, to be ready
Only when the yacht is sinking under you — step up into it
Straight after the MAYDAY, whatever the boat does
questions.why: A yacht afloat is a better liferaft: abandon only as a last resort, stepping up into the raft.

questions.q: A pan of oil catches fire on the galley stove. What do you do?
options: Open the hatch above to let the smoke out
Throw a jug of water over the pan
Carry the burning pan up to the cockpit
Turn off the gas and smother it with the fire blanket
questions.why: Water makes burning fat explode; cut the gas and smother the flames with the blanket.

questions.q: You have dropped the sails and motored back to the casualty. How do you make the final approach?
options: Slowly into the wind, engine off as you reach them
Across the wind, with them close to the stern
Downwind at speed, then hard astern beside them
Circle them fast until they catch a line
questions.why: Heading into the wind gives control at low speed; the propeller must be stopped near a person in the water.

questions.q: You are returning to a man overboard under sail. On which point of sail do you make the final approach?

figure.note: Under sail, coming back to the casualty

options: Close-hauled at full speed, sheets in hard
A close reach, easing sheets to stop beside them
A broad reach, sails full until alongside
A run, coming straight down onto them
questions.why: On a close reach you can spill wind to slow down and sheet in to speed up: full control of speed.

questions.q: You smell burning and see this as you motor along. How do you tackle the fire?

figure.title: Engine compartment
lines: Smoke coming from round the engine box
Extinguisher port in the box lid

options: Open the engine box wide to see the fire
Keep the engine running to reach harbour
Stop the engine, shut the fuel, discharge through the port
Pour sea water into the box with a bucket
questions.why: Stopping the engine and the fuel starves the fire; opening the box feeds it air.

questions.q: Where do you look first for the leak?
options: The deck hatches and the portlights
The cockpit lockers and the swim ladder
The mast foot and the anchor locker
Seacocks, hoses and the stern gland
questions.why: Water gets in fast through fittings below the waterline: seacocks, hose clips, the stern gland.

questions.q: You find a hose has come off a seacock below the waterline and the sea is pouring in. What do you do?
options: Close the seacock, or drive in the wooden bung
Stuff a towel round it and keep sailing
Call the lead boat and wait for advice
Start the bilge pump and head for harbour
questions.why: Stop the water at the source: close the valve; if it will not close, hammer in the tapered softwood bung.

questions.q: You hit an uncharted rock at 5 knots and stop, sitting on it. Nobody is hurt. What do you do before trying to get off?
options: Drive on ahead at full power over it
Check the bilge and hull for water coming in
Reverse off at full power straight away
Send the crew swimming to push her off
questions.why: If the hull is holed, the rock may be plugging it: find out before you pull off into deep water.

questions.q: The propeller is fouled and the engine has stopped. How do you carry on?

figure.title: Rope round the propeller
lines: Wind F3 off the land; harbour 2 M away

options: Dive under at once with the engine idling
Restart in reverse to unwind the rope
Leave the engine off, sail on and call the lead boat
Restart and run ahead hard to cut it free
questions.why: Restarting can wreck the shaft or gearbox: keep it off, sail, and get help to clear the rope.

questions.q: A shroud breaks and the mast goes over the side, banging against the hull. You want to use the engine. What do you do first?
options: Start the engine and tow the mast to harbour
Start the engine and hold her head to the sea
Start the engine and motor away from the rig
Get every rope and wire out of the water
questions.why: A trailing rope or wire will foul the propeller; start the engine only when nothing is in the water near it.

questions.q: You call the coastguard. Which call do you make?

figure.title: Crew injury
lines: Deep cut to the leg from a winch handle
Bleeding controlled with a pressure pad
Needs a doctor; the boat is fine

options: PAN-PAN — urgent, but no grave and imminent danger
MAYDAY — any injury aboard is a distress
SÉCURITÉ — it is a safety message
No call — wait for the evening harbour
questions.why: PAN-PAN is for urgent help, medical included; MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger to life or vessel.

questions.q: You need to raise the alarm. Which flare do you use?

figure.title: Night, disabled and drifting
lines: 8 M off the coast, VHF dead

options: A red hand flare
A red parachute rocket
An orange smoke signal
A white hand flare
questions.why: A parachute rocket goes up about 300 m and is seen from far off; hand flares pinpoint you once help is near.

questions.q: Your crew member has just been pulled back aboard. How do you warm them up?

figure.title: Recovered from the water
lines: April, sea 16 °C, 30 minutes in the water

options: Walk them briskly round the deck
Rub their arms and legs hard to warm them
Shelter, dry clothes, wrap them up, warm sweet drinks
A good tot of brandy to warm them up
questions.why: Warm gradually: out of the wind, dry layers and a sleeping bag; drinks only if alert, never alcohol.

questions.q: A crew member scalds a forearm with boiling water from the kettle. What do you do?
options: Hold ice straight on the skin for an hour
Smear butter or oil on it to soothe it
Burst the blisters, then cover it tightly
Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes
questions.why: Cool running water for 20 minutes limits the damage; then cover loosely with cling film or a clean dressing.

questions.q: You have run gently aground on sand. How do you try to get off?

figure.title: Aground
lines: Lead boat 1 M away, wind light

options: Reverse gently the way you came, crew to one side
Full ahead to drive over the bank
Wait for the tide to float you off tonight
Full astern and hold it, crew sitting still
questions.why: Back out along your own track; heeling the boat reduces draft. If that fails, call the lead boat — the Med tide will not help.

questions.q: The boom swings across in a gybe and strikes a crew member's head. They are knocked out for a few seconds, then say they feel fine. What do you do?
options: Nothing — they say they feel fine now
Get medical advice and watch them closely for hours
A stiff drink to help them over the shock
Painkillers and let them sleep it off alone
questions.why: Any knock-out needs medical advice; drowsiness, vomiting or confusion later can mean bleeding inside the skull.

questions.q: A crew member who has been on deck all day is in this state. What do you do for them?

figure.title: August, midday, no shade
lines: Crew member hot, red and dry-skinned

options: Give salt tablets and let them rest in the sun
Wrap them in a blanket to stop the shivering
Shade, cool with water and fanning, call for medical help
Let them sleep it off in the forecabin
questions.why: Hot dry skin and confusion mean heat stroke, a medical emergency: cool them fast and get help (PAN-PAN).

questions.q: The fire is now beyond your extinguishers. Which actions come next?

figure.title: Fire out of control
lines: 2 M offshore; lead boat 3 M away

options: Call the lead boat on the working channel and wait
Open all hatches to clear the smoke below
Everyone into the liferaft before any call
MAYDAY on 16, all on deck in lifejackets, raft ready
questions.why: A fire you cannot control is grave and imminent danger: MAYDAY first, then prepare to abandon.
